title: Multiply Strings
description:
# Multiply Strings

Given two non-negative integers `num1` and `num2` represented as strings, return the product of `num1` and `num2`, also represented as a string.

You must not use any built-in `BigInteger` library, and you must not convert an entire input string directly into a numeric type. Processing one digit, or a bounded fixed-width chunk, at a time is allowed.

## Example 1:

**Input:** num1 = "2", num2 = "3"
**Output:** "6"

## Example 2:

**Input:** num1 = "123", num2 = "456"
**Output:** "56088"

## Constraints:

* `1 <= num1.length, num2.length <= 200`
* `num1` and `num2` consist of digits only.
* Both `num1` and `num2` do not contain any leading zero, except the number 0 itself.

solutions.name: Grade School Multiplication
solutions.description:
## Approach

Allocate an integer array with `m + n` slots and simulate the multiplication table from right to left. The product of `num1[i]` and `num2[j]` contributes to positions `i + j` and `i + j + 1`, so each inner-loop step immediately stores the current digit and carries into the previous slot.

## Key Insight

The largest product of an `m`-digit and an `n`-digit number has at most `m + n` digits. Once that fixed array is available, every pair of digits has a deterministic output position and no full input ever needs to become an integer.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(m * n)
- Space Complexity: O(m + n)

solutions.name: Partial Products with String Addition
solutions.description:
## Approach

For every digit of `num2`, build the hand-written partial product against all digits of `num1`, append the positional zero shift, and add that partial product into a running string sum. The helper methods are the same multiplication-by-one-digit and addition routines used on paper.

## Key Insight

This route is intentionally close to manual multiplication. It is not the tightest implementation, but it teaches that big-number multiplication can be reduced to repeated single-digit multiplication plus string addition.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n * (m + n))
- Space Complexity: O(m + n)

solutions.name: Reversed Digit Convolution
solutions.description:
## Approach

Read both strings from low digit to high digit and accumulate each pairwise product into a reversed result array at index `(m - 1 - i) + (n - 1 - j)`. After all raw products are collected, perform one carry pass and reverse the digits to form the answer.

## Key Insight

The multiplication table is a digit convolution: every pair whose low-end offsets sum to the same value contributes to the same result digit before carries. Separating accumulation from carrying makes that structure visible.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(m * n)
- Space Complexity: O(m + n)

solutions.name: Base-10000 Chunk Multiplication
solutions.description:
## Approach

Split each input into fixed-width decimal chunks stored from least significant to most significant. Multiply every chunk pair into a `long` array using base 10000, then normalize carries and print the highest chunk normally while padding lower chunks to four digits.

## Key Insight

A bounded chunk is not the whole input number. Grouping four decimal digits at a time reduces loop iterations while preserving the same manual multiplication invariant and avoiding `BigInteger` or whole-input parsing.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(m * n)
- Space Complexity: O(m + n)

solutions.name: Karatsuba Divide and Conquer
solutions.description:
## Approach

Recursively split both decimal strings into high and low halves. Compute `z0 = lowA * lowB`, `z2 = highA * highB`, and `z1 = (lowA + highA) * (lowB + highB)`, then derive the cross term as `z1 - z2 - z0` and shift the three pieces back into decimal positions.

## Key Insight

Karatsuba replaces four half-size multiplications with three by recovering the two cross products together. It is an advanced route for this lesson because it uses the same string add, subtract, and decimal-shift building blocks but changes the multiplication structure.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^1.585)
- Space Complexity: O(n log n)
